transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-22
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (HelixScale CTO), Jenna (Lead Platform Engineer), Omar (SRE)

Summary (auto): HelixScale is evaluating Redwood for a mixed deployment: hosted for dev, dedicated for prod, private for regulated workloads. Key constraints: SOC2 compliance, KMS/HSM integration, VPC peering restrictions, 99ms p95 latency target for chat features. They use LangChain and LlamaIndex internally; ask about SDK examples and gateway/proxy pattern for multi-tenant routing and rate limits.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, im alex with redwood inference, im the ae on this one. we also have priya our se who will walk through integration options. hows everyone doing?
[00:12] Mark: good thanks, yeah appreciate it. we wanted to run through how you see us moving from dev to prod, and what the integration looks like. we have some security questions too.
[00:19] Priya: cool, can i do a super brief agenda? i'll sketch patterns for sdk usage, proxy/gateway approaches, and then typical rate-limiting + observability hooks and we can map to your constraints. sound ok?
[00:29] Mark: perfect.
[00:32] Jenna: quick context: helixscale runs a multi-tenant analytics platform, we ingest docs, build embeddings, then power a chat UI. we currently use an internal LLM cluster for embeddings and openai for chat while we evaluate alternatives. our stack: python microservices, langchain adapters, some llamaindex in pipelines, and k8s for infra.
[00:50] Omar: also to add, we have strict egress rules; anything that goes to third-party endpoints has to go via our egress proxy, and we may need VPC peering for high-volume flows.
[01:03] Alex: got it — sounds familiar. quick qualification: what's your target latency / cost tradeoff for chat? any SLOs?
[01:12] Mark: target p95 under 120ms for short responses, ideally 80-100ms. costs are a concern — we have a mid-market price sensitivity but will pay for SLA if it avoids incidents.
[01:24] Priya: ok, that steers us toward recommending dedicated for prod chat — gives predictable throughput and lower tail latency. hosted can be used for non-sensitive dev traffic. private (VPC/on-prem) is typically for regulated customers or data residency.
[01:38] Jenna: what's the operational difference? like network setup, and how much work for us to switch between modes?
[01:45] Priya: great question. hosted is the fastest onramp: api keys, sdk calls. Dedicated is a reserved gpu pool — you'll get a private endpoint and can tune autoscaling/burst policies. Private/VPC mode gives you a private control plane and optional on-prem runtime. Switching involves updating endpoints and, for private, additional network config (VPC peering, customer routing). our sdk is the same across modes so minimal code changes.
[02:10] Alex: we can share a migration checklist after.
[02:14] Mark: can you talk specifics about the sdk? we rely heavily on langchain and have bits of llamaindex.
[02:20] Priya: yes — our python and node sdks support direct calls for text generation, chat, and embeddings. we also publish examples for LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors; the pattern we recommend is keeping a thin gateway in your infra that handles auth, tenant routing, and rate quotas, then call redwood sdk from that layer. alternatively you can call redwood directly from services if you want less hop.
[02:45] Omar: we're concerned about leakage and token accounting — we need tenant-level quotas and token-level cost metrics. how granular are your metrics?
[02:53] Priya: we expose per-request metadata: tokens in/out, model variant used, model version, latency, and trace ids. you can emit these to your observability stack. we also have built-in tenant quotas at the Dedicated level — you set per-tenant rate and token budgets, and we enforce them.
[03:10] Jenna: is that enforced at the gateway or on the redwood side?
[03:14] Priya: on redwood's serving plane for dedicated/hosted — so enforcement is guaranteed even if a client bypasses your gateway. but many customers still put a local gateway for extra guardrails and compliance.
[03:26] Mark: what's the typical proxy pattern — sidecar, centralized gateway, or an edge proxy?
[03:31] Priya: all three are used. sidecar per pod is useful for per-request tracing and retries, centralized gateway helps with shared caching and tenant sharding, and edge proxies are good for egress control and IP allowlists. for HelixScale i'd recommend a centralized gateway in front of your microservices that handles auth and deduping, then let Redwood enforce quotas.
[03:50] Alex: to add: we have templates for proxy configs, and some customers use Envoy filters to add token masking and header injection.
[03:58] Omar: ok noted. how about langchain connectors — do you support streaming and function-calling-like features? our pipelines rely on streaming responses for low-latency user experience.
[04:10] Priya: yes, streaming is supported. we also have function/tool calling primitives — the SDK emits structured output which LangChain can handle with a small adapter. we'll send a LangChain example that demonstrates streaming + tool calling with our sdk.
[04:25] Mark: on security: SOC 2, SAML SSO for console, RBAC, and KMS for key management — we're going into our vendor risk assessment. can you outline exactly how keys are stored and whether customer keys can be used?
[04:38] Alex: we are SOC 2 Type II. For Hosted, we use KMS in our cloud provider but support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations for Dedicated/Private. audit logs and retention policies are configurable. we'll send the security pack and a network diagram.
[04:55] Jenna: is there an HSM-backed flow? our data classification requires HSM for certain PII work.
[05:01] Priya: yes, for Private deployments and some Dedicated contracts we can support HSM integrations. it's a contractual add-on and requires some config on the customer side as well — we can outline those steps in the security artifact.
[05:13] Omar: about data retention and logging — do you persist prompts and responses? and can we disable logging for certain routes?
[05:21] Priya: we persist metadata for observability and billing, and full payload retention is configurable. you can set routes to not persist payloads; also we have per-customer retention windows and exportable audit logs.
[05:34] Mark: great. switching back to perf — you mentioned KV cache and batching earlier — how does that affect latency for chat?
[05:41] Priya: two levers: continuous batching reduces per-token cost but can slightly add to latency; kv cache (prefix caching) drastically reduces tokens sent to the model for repeated context. with dedicated pools we tune the batching windows aggressively to keep p95 low. for your 80-100ms target, dedicated with tuned batching + prefix cache is the best bet.
[06:00] Mark: any numbers you can share for throughput per GPU or p95 for typical chat models?
[06:05] Priya: approximate — depends on model and sequence length; for a standard 2048-context open-weights variant on A100-ish class, you might see 150-300 reqs/s and p95 in 60-120ms with small responses. we'll share more precise benchmarks for the model variants you plan to use.
[06:22] Jenna: oh — we also use embeddings heavily and want to do reranking. is there a recommended pattern for embedding pipelines? run embeddings in batch and store vectors in our vector DB?
[06:33] Priya: yup, embeddings done in batch is common. we can also do streaming emb calls. many teams put embeddings into Pinecone/Weaviate/vector DB. for reranking, some customers use a smaller on-host model for first-pass scoring then call a larger model via Redwood for final scoring.
[06:48] Omar: about quotas again — can we set hard caps to protect against runaway costs during training or integration mistakes?
[06:55] Priya: yes — you can set hard token caps and rate caps per api-key/tenant. for Dedicated we have quota enforcement with webhooks for near-limit alerts. hosted also supports quotas but sandboxing/peering differs.
[07:08] Mark: what's the onboarding timeline if we want to get a dedicated pool configured?
[07:12] Alex: typical timeline is 2-4 weeks for small dedicated pools, depends on contract and network setup. Private on-prem takes longer — often 6-10 weeks.
[07:23] Jenna: do you provide a staging environment so we can run pre-prod smoke tests?
[07:27] Priya: yes — we provide a staging endpoint on the dedicated pool or can spin up a dev host for you to run smoke tests and perf runs.
[07:36] Mark: ok that's helpful. our next question: we use a custom auth token in headers and we need to propagate trace ids across the request path into your logs. is that supported?
[07:46] Priya: yes — pass a trace-id header and it gets surfaced in logs and telemetry. we can also instrument with OpenTelemetry for distributed traces if you want deeper correlation.
[07:56] Omar: one more operational thing: we use LlamaIndex heavily upstream. any gotchas integrating LlamaIndex with your sdk?
[08:03] Priya: LlamaIndex connectors typically work out of the box via our generic llm wrapper. the main gotchas are tokenization differences and ensuring you pin model versions. we'll include a LlamaIndex example that pins a model and shows caching.
[08:16] Mark: in terms of fallback and graceful degradation, what happens if the dedicated pool is saturated? do you fall back to hosted or queue?
[08:24] Alex: we support automatic fallback policies — you can configure to fail fast, queue (within limits), or fallback to a cheaper hosted variant. fallbacks preserve the api contract but note that model variants may change outputs.
[08:36] Jenna: how do you handle model rollouts and version pinning? we need stable behavior for A/B tests.
[08:42] Priya: model pinning is supported per-route. rollouts can be canary or weighted, and you can tie them to experiments. there's also regression monitoring built in to alert on quality drift for specified eval prompts.
[08:55] Mark: that eval monitoring sounds good. do you integrate with our existing monitoring stack? we use prometheus + grafana, and datadog for traces.
[09:04] Priya: metrics export via prometheus and traces via OTLP are supported. we also have a webhook for alerts and an api to pull token-cost breakdowns.
[09:14] Omar: ok can we talk briefly about egress — our security team requires all third-party network calls to go through a customer-managed NAT and egress proxy. how would that work with dedicated?
[09:26] Alex: for Dedicated we can either peer into your VPC so calls stay within the peered network, or you can use egress proxies to route traffic; for hosting we have to follow public endpoints. peering is the recommended option for heavy traffic.
[09:39] Mark: are there extra costs for peering?
[09:41] Alex: usually there's a small networking charge to cover private link setup — depends on the cloud provider. we'll include estimated networking fees in the pricing packet.
[09:51] Jenna: one more rate question — can we do per-route quotas, like treat embeddings differently from chat?
[09:58] Priya: yes per-route quotas and token budgets are common. you can also define per-model policies so embeddings and chat have separate caps and alerts.
[10:07] Mark: cool. thinking about pilot sizing — we proposed 30k tokens/day to start and then scale. can Redwood throttle gracefully if we exceed pilot budgets?
[10:17] Priya: yes, throttling and hard caps apply. we also provide webhook notifications and an api to programmatically top up quotas.
[10:25] Omar: if we do a private on-prem deployment, what telemetry do we still see in your console? any limitations?
[10:33] Priya: for private with customer-controlled plane, you get the same telemetry but can choose what to share with Redwood support. in air-gapped setups you might need to push logs to a s3 bucket or to your own observability endpoint. some remote debugging features are limited unless you enable secure connectivity.
[10:54] Mark: ok, lets talk about sample integration — can you walk through a tiny flow: user asks chat -> service builds prompt with history -> we call langchain -> redwood call -> response -> render. what are the headers and token accounting steps?
[11:12] Priya: sure — at a high level: 1) user request hits your gateway; 2) computed prompt + history is assembled, with kernel items flagged for function-calls if any; 3) gateway injects tenant-id, api-key and trace-id headers; 4) call redwood sdk generate/chat endpoint; 5) redwood responds with tokens, model, and trace id; 6) your service records tokens for billing and observability. The SDK returns token counts which you can store.
[11:43] Jenna: do you do automatic prompt truncation or do we need to manage that?
[11:47] Priya: SDK can help with prompt trimming utilities, but many teams implement application-aware truncation to preserve important context. we have examples in the sdk utils.
[11:58] Mark: any recommended quantization or model advice if we want to reduce costs for reranking?
[12:03] Priya: quantized model variants are great for cost reduction on embeddings/first-pass ranking. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles by workload; we'll include a set of suggested configs.
[12:18] Omar: you mentioned prefix/KV cache earlier — if we have many similar conversations, can the cache be shared across tenants or is it per-tenant?
[12:27] Priya: caches are per-tenant to avoid data leakage. shared caches would be a big no for multi-tenant safety.
[12:34] Mark: let's talk about the pilot timeline and metrics. what should success look like?
[12:39] Priya: success criteria: latency p95 under 120ms for chat, stable throughput at target QPS, correct token accounting, successful enforcement of quotas, and no security blockers from your vendor assessment. we'll help run a perf test and provide logs.
[12:53] Alex: ok maybe time for questions from your security/infra team — anything else?
[12:58] Mark: just clarifying the SOC2 artifacts and whether we can do a security phone call with your compliance team.
[13:06] Alex: yes we can schedule a security deep dive. i'll include compliance contacts in the pack.
[13:11] Jenna: and can you share the sample LangChain connector repo link?
[13:15] Priya: yes we'll push a repo and a short README showing streaming + function calls + token accounting.
[13:23] Omar: final thought — do you support request-level encryption with customer keys? we need to encrypt payloads at rest with our key.
[13:31] Alex: yes customer-managed KMS/hsm for dedicated/private supports that for data at rest; request-level envelope encryption is something we'd scope as part of private/on-prem. we'll flag that as an advanced requirement.
[13:44] Mark: thanks — this was really clarifying. can we recap next steps?
[13:49] Alex: recap: 1) redwood will send security pack, network diagram, and compliance contacts (alex) 2) priya will share sdk + langchain/llamaindex examples and a small demo repo (priya) 3) helixscale shares traffic profile and egress constraints (jenna/omar) 4) schedule pilot for early june targeting dedicated pool; security deep dive to be scheduled.
[14:12] Mark: that matches.
[14:14] Priya: any other blockers?
[14:16] Jenna: no, just internal alignment.
[14:18] Omar: none from me.
[14:20] Alex: awesome — we'll follow up with the artifacts by next week. thanks everyone.
[14:26] Mark: thanks all.
